<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{p:1}
Let $X$ be a Hausdorff space and $x\in X$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
If $X$ is a homogeneous space, then $\operatorname{sp}_t(x,X)=\operatorname{sp}_t(X)$.
\item
If $x\in K\subset X$, then $\operatorname{sp}_t(x,K)\subset \operatorname{sp}_t(x,X)$ and $\operatorname{sp}_t(K)\subset \operatorname{sp}_t(X)$.
\item
If $X$ is an infinite compact space, then $\operatorname{sp}_t(X)$ contains all infinite regular cardinals not exceeding $t(X)$.
\item
If $X$ is an infinite compact space, then $\omega\in \operatorname{sp}_t(X)$.
\item
If $x$ is a non-isolated point, then
\begin{align*}
wt(x,X)&=\min \operatorname{sp}_t(x,X),
&
t(x,X)&=\sup \operatorname{sp}_t(x,X).
\end{align*}
\item
$|\operatorname{sp}_t(x,X)|\leq 1$ if and only if $wt(x,X)=t(x,X)$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
(1) and (2) are obvious.

(3) Let $\tau=t(X)$. Since $X$ is compact, there is a free sequence $\bbsetx_\alpha:\alpha<\tau\eeset\subset X$ \cite[Theorem 7.12]{Hodel1984handbook}.
Let $\mu\leq\tau$ be an infinite regular cardinal and let $y$ be a complete accumulation point of the set $A=\bbsetx_\alpha:\alpha<\mu\eeset$. Then $\mu=T(y,A)\in \operatorname{sp}_t(X)$.

(4) There is a countable $A\subset X$ and $y\in \overline{A}\setminus A$. Then $\omega=T(y,A)\in \operatorname{sp}_t(X)$.

(5) is obvious. (6) follows from (5).
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{p:1-1}
Let $X$ be a Hausdorff space, $x\in X$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
If $x$ is a \wob/-point, then
\[
\chi(x,X)=\pi\chi(x,X)=\psi(x,X)=t(x,X)=wt(x,X)=P(x,X).
\]
\item
If $\chi(x,X)=P(x,X)$, then $x$ is a \wob/-point.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
(1) Let $\lambda=P(x,X)$. It suffices to show that $\chi(x,X)\leq \lambda$.
Let ${\mathcal U}$ be a linearly ordered base of $x$ and let $\bbsetV_\alpha:\alpha<\lambda\eeset$ be a system of neighbourhoods of $x$ with $x\notin \operatorname{Int} \bigcap_{\alpha<\lambda}V_\alpha$. Take ${\mathcal O}=\bbsetU_\alpha:\alpha<\lambda\eeset\subset {\mathcal U}$ such that $U_\alpha\subset V_\alpha$ and $U_\alpha\supset U_\beta$ for $\alpha<\beta<\lambda$. Then ${\mathcal O}$ is a base at $x$.

(2) Let $\lambda=P(x,X)$. Let $\bbsetW_\alpha:\alpha<\lambda\eeset$ be a base of $x$ and let $\bbsetV_\alpha:\alpha<\lambda\eeset$ be a system of neighbourhoods of $x$ with $x\notin \operatorname{Int} \bigcap_{\alpha<\lambda}V_\alpha$. 
Let ${\mathcal U}=\bbsetU_\alpha:\alpha<\lambda\eeset$ be a family of open subsets of $X$ such that $U_\alpha\subset W_\alpha\cap V_\alpha$ and $U_\alpha\supset U_\beta$ for $\alpha<\beta<\gamma$. Then ${\mathcal U}$ is a linear base at $x$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{p:1+0}
Let $Y$ be a LOTS and $x\in X\subset Y$.
On $X$ we consider the order inherited from $Y$ and the subspace topology of the space $Y$.
Denote $L_*=X\cap \lL(x,Y)$, $R_*=X\cap \lR(x,Y)$, $L=L_*\cup \{x\}$, $R=R_*\cup \{x\}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
The point $x$ in $L$ is a \wob/-point. If $x\in \overline{L_*}$, then $\chi(x,L)=\operatorname{cf}_l(x,X)=\operatorname{cf}_l(x,Y)$.
\item
The point $x$ in $R$ is a \wob/-point. If $x\in \overline{R_*}$, then $\chi(x,R)=\operatorname{cf}_r(x,X)=\operatorname{cf}_r(x,Y)$.
\item
The point $x$ in $X$ is a \wob/-point if and only if one of the following conditions holds:
\begin{enumerate}
      
                                                                                     
\item
$x\notin \overline{L_*}$;
\item
$x\notin \overline{R_*}$;
\item
$x\in \overline{L_*}\cap \overline{R_*}$ and $\operatorname{cf}_l(x,X)=\operatorname{cf}_r(x,X)$.
\end{enumerate}
\item
              
\begin{enumerate}
\item
$\operatorname{sp}_t(x,X)=\varnothing$ if 
$x\notin \overline{L_*}$ and $x\notin \overline{R_*}$, that is, $x$ is an isolated point of $X$;
\item
$\operatorname{sp}_t(x,X)=\{\operatorname{cf}_l(x,X)\}$ 
if $x\in \overline{L_*}$ and $x\notin \overline{R_*}$;
\item
$\operatorname{sp}_t(x,X)=\{\operatorname{cf}_r(x,X)\}$ 
if $x\notin \overline{L_*}$ and $x\in \overline{R_*}$;
\item
$\operatorname{sp}_t(x,X)=\{\operatorname{cf}_l(x,X),\operatorname{cf}_r(x,X)\}$ 
if $x\in \overline{L_*}$ and $x\in \overline{R_*}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Let us prove (1).
Let $\lambda=\operatorname{cf}_l(x,X)$ and let $\bbsetx_\alpha:\alpha<\lambda\eeset$ be a set cofinal in $L_*$. Then
the family $\bbset\ilpc(x_\alpha,x]:\alpha<\lambda\eeset$ forms a base of $x$ in $\ilpc(-\infty, x]$, and
the family $\bbset\ilpc(x_\alpha,x]\cap X:\alpha<\lambda\eeset$ forms a base of $x$ in $L$.

Item (2) follows from (1).

Let us prove (3). ($\Leftarrow$) 
Item (a) follows from (2). Item (b) follows from (1).
Let us prove (c). Let $\lambda=\operatorname{cf}_l(x,X)$, let $\bbsetx_\alpha:\alpha<\gamma\eeset\subset L_*$ be a sequence increasing to $x$, and let $\bbsety_\alpha:\alpha<\gamma\eeset\subset R_*$ be a sequence decreasing to $x$.
Then $\bbset\ilpp(x_\alpha,y_\alpha)\cap X:\alpha<\gamma\eeset$ is a linearly ordered base at the point $x$.

($\Rightarrow$) If $x\notin \overline{L_*}$ or $x\notin \overline{R_*}$, then either (a) or (b) holds.
Consider the case $x\in \overline{L_*}\cap \overline{R_*}$. There is a linearly ordered base $\bbset\ilpp(x_\alpha,y_\lambda)\cap X:\alpha<\lambda\eeset$ of $x$, where $\lambda$ is some regular cardinal and $x_\alpha\in L_*$, $y_\alpha\in R_*$ for $\alpha<\lambda$. Then $\lambda=\operatorname{cf}_l(x,X)=\operatorname{cf}_r(x,X)$, and (d) holds.

Item (4) is obvious.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{p:1+0.5}
Let $X$ be a LOTS and $x\in X$. If $x$ is a minimum, a maximum, or a jump point, then $x$ is a \wob/-point.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{p:1+1}
Let $X$ be a GO space and $x\in X$.
Then  
                            
\begin{align*}
\pi\chi(x,X) &= wt(x,X)= P(x,X),
&
\chi(x,X) &= \psi(x,X) = t(x,X).
\end{align*}
If $x$ is not an isolated point of $X$, then
\begin{align*}
\min \operatorname{sp}_t(x,X) &= \pi\chi(x,X),
&
\max \operatorname{sp}_t(x,X) &= \chi(x,X).
\end{align*}
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
The proposition is obvious if $x$ is an isolated point. Consider the case when $x$ is not an isolated point. Then $\operatorname{sp}_t(x,X)\neq\varnothing$.

If $|\operatorname{sp}_t(x,X)|=1$, then $\min \operatorname{sp}_t(x,X)=\max \operatorname{sp}_t(x,X)$, and Proposition \ref{p:1+0}(3) implies that $x$ is a \wob/-point. The required equality then follows from Proposition \ref{p:1-1} and Proposition \ref{p:1+0}(1,2).

Consider the case $|\operatorname{sp}_t(x,X)|>1$.
Let $Y$ be a LOTS in which $X$ is embedded.
On $X$ we consider the order inherited from $Y$.
Denote $L_*=X\cap \lL(x,Y)$, $R_*=X\cap \lR(x,Y)$, $L=L_*\cup \{x\}$, $R=R_*\cup \{x\}$, $\lambda=\operatorname{cf}_l(x,X)$, $\rho=\operatorname{cf}_r(x,X)$.
By Proposition \ref{p:1+0}(4), $x\in \overline{L_*}\cap \overline{R_*}$, $|\operatorname{sp}_t(x,X)|=2$, and $\operatorname{sp}_t(x,X)=\{\lambda,\rho\}$. Without loss of generality $\lambda<\rho$. Then $\lambda=\min \operatorname{sp}_t(x,X)$ and $\rho=\max \operatorname{sp}_t(x,X)$. By Proposition \ref{p:1+0}(1,2), $x$ is a \wob/-point in $L$ and in $R$.
By Proposition \ref{p:1-1}, $\pi\chi(x,L) = wt(x,L)= P(x,L)=\lambda$ and $\pi\chi(x,R) = wt(x,R)= P(x,R)=\rho>\lambda$. Hence $\pi\chi(x,X) = wt(x,X)= P(x,X)=\lambda$.

By Proposition \ref{p:1-1}, $\chi(x,L) = t(x,L)= \psi(x,L)=\lambda<\rho$ and $\chi(x,R) = t(x,R)= \psi(x,R)=\rho$. Hence $\chi(x,X)= \psi(x,X) = t(x,X) = \rho$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{p:1+1.5}
Let $X$ be a LOTS and $x\in X$. Then
\begin{align*}
\pi\chi(x,X) &= \omega + \min \operatorname{cf}_l(x,X), \operatorname{cf}_r(x,X),
\\
\chi(x,X) &=  \omega + \max \operatorname{cf}_l(x,X), \operatorname{cf}_r(x,X).
\end{align*}
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{p:1+2}
Let $X$ be a GO space and $x\in X$.
The following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item
$x$ is a \wob/-point;
\item
$\chi(x,X)= \pi\chi(x,X)$;
\item
$|\operatorname{sp}_t(x,X)|\leq 1$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{p:1+3}
In a monotonically normal compact space the set of \wob/-points is dense.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- cor-1: body_md -->
\label{c:cfgos:1}
In a compact LOTS the set of \wob/-points is dense.
<!-- end cor-1 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Let $X$ be a compact LOTS. Let $U$ be a nonempty open subset of $X$.
Isolated points of $U$ are \wob/-points. Consider the case when $U$ has no isolated points.
Set ${\mathcal I}=\bbset\ilpp(a,b): a,b\in U,\ \varnothing\neq\ilpp(a,b)\subset U\eeset$. On ${\mathcal I}$ consider the order: for $A,B\in {\mathcal I}$, $A<B$ if $\overline{B}\subset A$.
By the Hausdorff maximum principle there is a maximal linearly ordered subset ${\mathcal U}\subset {\mathcal I}$. Let $F=\bigcap{\mathcal U}$. Then $F\neq\varnothing$. Let $a=\min F$ and $b=\max F$.

Let us show that $\ilpp(a,b)=\varnothing$. Suppose otherwise. Since $U$ has no isolated points, the set $\ilpp(a,b)$ is infinite. Let $a',c,b'\in \ilpp(a,b)$, $a'<c<b'$. Then $I=\ilpp(a',b')\in {\mathcal I}$ and $A<I$ for every $A\in {\mathcal U}$, contradicting the maximality of ${\mathcal U}$. Thus $\ilpp(a,b)=\varnothing$.

If $a=b$, then $F=\{a\}$ and ${\mathcal U}$ is a linearly ordered base of the point $a$. If $a\neq b$, then $a$ and $b$ are jump points. By Proposition \ref{p:1+0.5}, $a$ and $b$ are \wob/-points.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{p:1+0a}
Let $Y$ be a LOTS, $X\subset Y$.
On $X$ we consider the order inherited from $Y$ and the subspace topology of the space $Y$.
Let $L_x=\ilpp(-\infty,x)\cap X$ and $R_x=\ilpp(x,+\infty)\cap X$ for $x\in X$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
The topology of $X$ coincides with the order topology on $X$ if and only if
for every $x\in X$ the following conditions hold:
\begin{enumerate}
\item
$\max L_x$ exists if $x\notin\overline{L_x}$;
\item
$\min R_x$ exists if $x\notin\overline{R_x}$.
\end{enumerate}
\item
The topology of $X$ coincides with the order topology on $X$ if
one of the following conditions holds:
\begin{enumerate}
\item
$x\in \overline{L_x}\cap \overline{R_x}$ for every $x\in X$;
\item
$X$ is dense in $Y$ and contains no jump points of $Y$;
\item
$X$ is compact.
\end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Item (1) is verified directly without difficulty. Item (2) follows from (1).
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{p:1+4}
Let $X$ be a LOTS.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
The space $X$ is locally compact if $X$ has no gaps.
\item
The space $X$ is compact if and only if $X$ has no gaps and $X$ has a minimum and a maximum.
\item
The space $X$ is connected if and only if $X$ has no gaps and no jumps.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{p:1+5}
Let $X$ be a compact LOTS.
The space $X$ is zero-dimensional if and only if for any $a,b\in X$, $a<b$, there is a jump $(A,B)$ such that $\ilpc(-\infty,a]\subset A$ and $\ilcp[b,+\infty)\subset B$.
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
($\Rightarrow$) Let $a<b$. Since $X$ is a zero-dimensional compact space, there is a clopen $U\subset X$ such that $\ilpc(-\infty,a]\subset U$ and $\ilcp[b,+\infty)\subset X\setminus A$. Set $a'=\max U$. Then the set $\ilpc(-\infty,a']$ is clopen.
Set $b'=\min \ilpp(a',+\infty)$, $A=\ilpc(-\infty,a']$ and $B=\ilcp[b,+\infty)$.
Then $(A,B)$ is a jump and $\ilpc(-\infty,a]\subset A$ and $\ilcp[b,+\infty)\subset B$.

($\Leftarrow$) The condition implies that $X$ is totally disconnected. Since $X$ is compact, $X$ is zero-dimensional \cite[Theorem 6.2.9]{EngelkingBookRu}.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
\label{p:1+6}
Let $X$ be a zero-dimensional compact LOTS. A base at a point $x\in X$ is formed by open intervals of the form $\ilcc[a,b]$, where $a$ is the minimum of $X$ or a right jump point, and $b$ is the maximum of $X$ or a left jump point.
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Let $U$ be an open interval containing $x$.

Let us find the point $a$.
If $\ilpp(-\infty,x)\cap U=\varnothing$, set $a=x$. Otherwise, take $a'\in \ilpp(-\infty,x)\cap U$. By Proposition \ref{p:1+5} there exist $a'',a\in X$ such that $a'\leq a''<a\leq x$ and $\ilpp(a'',a)=\varnothing$.

Let us find the point $b$.
If $\ilpp(x,+\infty)\cap U=\varnothing$, set $b=x$. Otherwise, take $b'\in \ilpp(x,+\infty)\cap U$. By Proposition \ref{p:1+5} there exist $b'',b\in X$ such that $x\leq b<b''\leq b'$ and $\ilpp(b,b'')=\varnothing$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{t:main:1}
Let $X$ be a homogeneous GO space. Then
\begin{enumerate}
\item
$\chi(K)\leq\omega_1$ and $|K|\leq 2^{\omega_1}$ for every compact $K\subset X$;
\item
if there is a compact $K\subset X$ with $\chi(K)>\omega$, then $\chi(X)=\omega_1$ and $\pi\chi(X)=\omega$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Let $K\subset X$ be compact.
By Proposition \ref{p:1+0}(4) and Proposition \ref{p:1}(1), $|\operatorname{sp}_t(X)|\leq 2$.
By Proposition \ref{p:1}(2), $\operatorname{sp}_t(K)\subset \operatorname{sp}_t(X)$, hence $|\operatorname{sp}_t(K)|\leq 2$.
By Proposition \ref{p:1+0}(3), $\operatorname{sp}_t(K)\subset\{\omega,\omega_1\}$.

Let us prove (1). If $K$ is finite, the statement is obvious. Consider the case when $K$ is infinite.
By Proposition \ref{p:1+1}, $\chi(K)=\max \operatorname{sp}_t(K)\leq \omega_1$.
By the Arhangel'skii theorem
\cite[Theorem 4.5]{Hodel1984handbook}, $|K|\leq 2^{\omega_1}$.

Let us prove (2). Let $\chi(K)>\omega$. By (1), $\chi(K)=\omega_1\in \operatorname{sp}_t(K)$.
By Proposition \ref{p:1}(4), $\omega\in \operatorname{sp}_t(K)$. Since $\operatorname{sp}_t(K)\subset\{\omega,\omega_1\}$, we get $\operatorname{sp}_t(K)=\{\omega,\omega_1\}$. Since $\operatorname{sp}_t(K)\subset \operatorname{sp}_t(X)$ and $|\operatorname{sp}_t(X)|\leq 2$, we get $\operatorname{sp}_t(X)=\{\omega,\omega_1\}$. By Proposition \ref{p:1+1}, $\chi(X)=\omega_1$ and $\pi\chi(X)=\omega$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proposition-13: body_md -->
\label{p:main:1}
Let $\lambda$ be a regular cardinal and $C\subset \lambda$ a stationary subset. Then $\Delta(C)=\lambda$.
<!-- end proposition-13 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Since $|C|=\lambda$, we have $\Delta(C)\leq\lambda$. Suppose $\Delta(C)\neq\lambda$. Then there is a family $\mathcal{W}$ of open neighbourhoods of the diagonal $\Delta_C$ in the square $C\times C$ such that $\bigcap\mathcal{W}=\Delta_C$ and $|\mathcal{W}|<\lambda$.

For $W\in\mathcal{W}$ find $x_W\in C$ such that $U_W\times U_W\subset W$, where $U_W=\bbsetx\in C: x> x_W\eeset$. Let $c_0=\min C$ and $C_*=C\setminus \{c_0\}$. For each $x\in C_*$ there is $f(x)\in C$, $f(x)<x$, such that $V_x \times V_x\subset W$, where $V_x=\bbsety\in C: f(x)< y \leq x\eeset$. By Fodor's lemma, the set $f^{-1}(x_W)$ is stationary in $\lambda$ for some $x_W\in C$. Then $U_W\times U_W=\bigcup_{x\in f^{-1}(x_W)}V_x\times V_x\subset W$.

Since $\lambda$ is a regular cardinal and $|\mathcal{W}|<\lambda$, there is $a\in C$ such that $x_W<a$ for all $W\in \mathcal{W}$. Take $b\in C$, $a<b$. Then $(a,b)\notin \Delta_C$ and $(a,b)\in W$ for all $W\in\mathcal{W}$, contradicting $\bigcap\mathcal{W}=\Delta_C$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{t:main:1+1}
Let $G$ be a semitopological group that is a GO space.
Then $G$ is hereditarily paracompact and
\[
P(X) = wt(X)= \pi\chi(X) = \Delta(X) =
\chi(X) = \psi(X) = t(X).
\]
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Let $\tau=P(X)$. By Proposition \ref{p:1+1} and the homogeneity of $X$, $wt(X)= \pi\chi(X) = \tau$.
Since $G$ is a semitopological group and $\pi\chi(X) = \tau$, we get $\Delta(X)\leq\tau$ (\cite[Theorem 1]{Reznichenko2023-1}, \cite[Theorem 2.4]{arh-rezn2005}, and \cite[Corollary 5.7.5]{at2009} for countable $\tau$). Since $\psi(X)\leq \Delta(X)$, Proposition \ref{p:1+1} and the homogeneity of $X$ give $\chi(X) = t(X) = \psi(X) \leq \Delta(X)\leq \tau$. Since $\pi\chi(X)\leq \chi(X)$, we get $\chi(X) = t(X) = \psi(X) = \Delta(X) = \tau$.

Let us prove that $G$ is hereditarily paracompact. Suppose otherwise. Since a GO space is monotonically normal, $G$ is a monotonically normal, non-hereditarily-paracompact space. By \cite[Theorem I]{BaloghRudin1992}, there is a regular cardinal $\lambda$ and a stationary subset $C\subset \lambda$ homeomorphic to some $F\subset G$. By Proposition \ref{p:main:1}, $\Delta(F)=\lambda$. Since $\Delta(F)\leq \Delta(X)$, we get $\lambda\leq \tau$. A stationary subset is not discrete, so let $x\in F$ be a non-isolated point of $F$. Then $\tau=wt(x,X)\leq T(x,F\setminus\{x\})<\lambda$, contradicting $\lambda\leq \tau$.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{t:main:2}
Let $G$ be a semitopological group that is a GO space and not a $P$-space.
Then $G$ has countable character, is submetrizable, and is hereditarily paracompact.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Since $G$ is not a $P$-space, $P(x,G)=\omega$ for some $x\in G$.
By Theorem \ref{t:main:1+1}, $\chi(G)=\Delta(G)=\omega$ and $G$ is hereditarily paracompact.
Paracompact spaces with a $G_\delta$-diagonal are submetrizable \cite[Corollary 2.9]{gru1984}.
Note also that GO spaces with a $G_\delta$-diagonal are (hereditarily) paracompact \cite[Theorem 4.5]{Lutzer1971}.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- cor-2: body_md -->
\label{с:main:1}
In semitopological GO groups compact subsets are metrizable.
<!-- end cor-2 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{t:main:3}
Let $G$ be a semitopological group that is a LOTS and not a $P$-space.
Then $G$ is metrizable.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
By Theorem \ref{t:main:2}, $G$ has a $G_\delta$-diagonal.
A LOTS with a $G_\delta$-diagonal is metrizable \cite{Lutzer1969}, \cite[Theorem 2.3]{gru1984}.
Hence $G$ is metrizable.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{t:main:3+1}
Let $G$ be a monotonically normal paratopological group. Then $G$ is hereditarily paracompact and every compact subset of $G$ has countable tightness.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Monotonically normal paratopological groups are hereditarily paracompact \cite[Theorem 2.6]{BuzyakovaVural2014}, and hence compact subsets of such groups have countable tightness \cite[Theorem 3.5]{WilliamsZhou1998}.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{t:main:2+1}
Let $G$ be a topological group that is a GO space and not a $P$-space.
Then $G$ is metrizable.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
By Theorem \ref{t:main:2}, $G$ has countable character. Since $G$ has countable character, the Birkhoff--Kakutani theorem \cite[Theorem 3.3.12]{at2009} implies that the group $G$ is metrizable.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{t:cssoh:1}
Let $X$ be an order-homogeneous LOTS.
Then every compact subset of $X$ is first countable.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Let $K\subset X$ be compact. Suppose $\chi(K)>\omega$. Then $\omega_1+1$ embeds monotonically in $K$. Without loss of generality, let $f: \omega_1+1 \to K$ be an increasing embedding. Then $\omega=\operatorname{cf}_l(f(\omega),X)\neq \operatorname{cf}_l(f(\omega_1),X)=\omega_1$, contradicting the order-homogeneity of $X$.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- proposition-14: body_md -->
\label{p:2}
If $X$ is a linearly ordered set with no greatest and no least element, $\lambda$ is a limit ordinal, and $f\inX^{\lambda}$, then the family $\bbset\mathfrak{B}_{X}(f,\alpha): \alpha<\lambda\eeset$ forms a base of open neighbourhoods of the point $f$ in the linearly ordered space $X^{\lambda}$.
<!-- end proposition-14 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Let us show that the set $\mathfrak{B}_{X}(f,\alpha)$ is open. Let $g\in \mathfrak{B}_{X}(f,\alpha)$. There exist $a,b\in \mathfrak{B}_{X}(f,\alpha)$ such that $a(\alpha)<g(\alpha)<b(\alpha)$. Then $g\in (a,b)\subset \mathfrak{B}_{X}(f,\alpha)$.

Let us show that the family $\bbset\mathfrak{B}_{X}(f,\alpha): \alpha<\lambda\eeset$ forms a base of neighbourhoods of $f$. Let $a,b\in X^{\lambda}$ and $a< f <b$. Let $\alpha=\min\bbset\delta<\lambda: a(\delta)\neq f(\delta)\eeset$, $\beta=\min\bbset\delta<\lambda: b(\delta)\neq f(\delta)\eeset$, $\theta=\max \alpha,\beta$. Then $f\in \mathfrak{B}_{X}(f,\theta+1)\subset (a,b)$.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- proposition-15: body_md -->
\label{p:h:tg1}
                             
Let $\lambda$ be a regular cardinal and $G=\mathbb R^{\lambda}$ with the order topology.
Then $G$ is a LOTS topological group and $\chi(G)=\lambda$.
The space $G$ is a $P_\lambda$-space.
<!-- end proposition-15 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
On $G$ we consider the group operation induced from $\mathbb R^\lambda$, addition of functions. By Proposition \ref{p:2}, the family of open subgroups $\bbset\mathfrak{B}_{\mathbb R}(0,\alpha): \alpha<\lambda\eeset$ forms a base of neighbourhoods of the zero function.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- proposition-16: body_md -->
\label{p:h:1}
Let $\lambda$ be an ordinal and $X$ a compact LOTS.
Then the LOTS $X^{\lambda}$ is compact.
<!-- end proposition-16 -->
<!-- proposition-17: body_md -->
\label{p:blex:1}
Let $\lambda$ be a regular cardinal, $x\in \mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$, $\kappa_0=\operatorname{cf} x^{-1}(0)$ and $\kappa_1=\operatorname{cf} x^{-1}(1)$. Then 
\begin{enumerate}
\item
$\operatorname{cf}_l(x,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\kappa_1$, $\operatorname{cf}_r(x,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\kappa_0$, and $\lambda\in\{\kappa_0,\kappa_1\}$;
\item
$\chi(x,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\lambda$, 
\[
\pi\chi(x,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\begin{cases}
\min \{\kappa_0, \kappa_1\}, & \kappa_0\text{ and }\kappa_1\text{  are infinite,}
\\
\lambda, & \kappa_0\text{ or }\kappa_1\text{ is finite.}
\end{cases}
\]
\item
the point $x$ is a \wob/-point if and only if one of the following conditions holds:
\begin{enumerate}
\item
$|x^{-1}(0)|=|x^{-1}(1)|=\lambda$;
\item
$x^{-1}(0) =\varnothing$  or $x^{-1}(1) =\varnothing$;
\item
the set $x^{-1}(0)$ has a maximum;
\item
the set $x^{-1}(1)$ has a maximum.
\end{enumerate}
\item
the point $x$ is a left jump point if and only if the set $x^{-1}(0)$ has a maximum; denoting $\mu = \max x^{-1}(0)$, in this case $x=\ensuremath{\left.x\right|_{\mu}} \mathbin{{}^\frown} 0 \mathbin{{}^\frown} 1_\lambda$ and $r=\ensuremath{\left.x\right|_{\mu}} \mathbin{{}^\frown} 1 \mathbin{{}^\frown} 0_\lambda$ is the right jump point;
\item
the point $x$ is a right jump point if and only if the set $x^{-1}(1)$ has a maximum; denoting $\mu = \max x^{-1}(0)$, in this case $x=\ensuremath{\left.x\right|_{\mu}} \mathbin{{}^\frown} 1 \mathbin{{}^\frown} 0_\lambda$ and $l=\ensuremath{\left.x\right|_{\mu}} \mathbin{{}^\frown} 0 \mathbin{{}^\frown} 1_\lambda$ is the left jump point.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-17 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Let us prove (1). Since $\lambda$ is a regular cardinal and $\lambda=x^{-1}(0)\cup x^{-1}(1)$, either $\kappa_0=\lambda$ or $\kappa_1=\lambda$.
Denote $M=x^{-1}(1)$. Then $\kappa_1=\operatorname{cf} M$.

If $\kappa_1=0$, then $x=0_\lambda$ and $\operatorname{cf}_l(x,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\kappa_1=0$.

Consider the case $\kappa_1=1$. Then $\mu=\max M$ exists.
Set $l=\ensuremath{\left.x\right|_{\mu}} \mathbin{{}^\frown} 0 \mathbin{{}^\frown} 1_\lambda$.
Then $l$ is a left jump point, $x$ is a right jump point, $l=\max \ilpp(-\infty,x)$, and $\operatorname{cf}_l(x,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\kappa_1=1$.

Consider the case $\kappa_1\geq\omega$.
Let $\bbset\eta_\alpha:\alpha<\kappa_1\eeset\subset M$ be a strictly increasing cofinal sequence.
For $\alpha<\kappa_1$ define $y_\alpha\in \mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$:
\begin{equation*}
y_\alpha(\nu) = 
\begin{cases}
x(\nu),	& \nu\neq \eta_\alpha; 
\\
0,	& \nu= \eta_\alpha.
\end{cases}
\end{equation*}
Then the strictly increasing sequence $\bbsety_\alpha:\alpha<\kappa\eeset\subset \lL(x,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})$ converges to $x$.
Hence $\operatorname{cf}_l(x,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\kappa_1$.

Since $x^{-1}(0)=\left(R_\lambda(x)\right)^{-1}(1)$, we have
\[
\operatorname{cf}_r(x,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\operatorname{cf}_l(R_\lambda(x),\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\operatorname{cf} \left(R_\lambda(x)\right)^{-1}(1)= \operatorname{cf} x^{-1}(0)=\kappa_0.
\]

Let us prove (2). By (1) and Propositions \ref{p:1+0} and \ref{p:1+1}, $\chi(x,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\lambda$. If $\kappa_0$ or $\kappa_1$ is finite, then $\operatorname{sp}_t(\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\{\lambda\}$, and by Proposition \ref{p:1+1}, $\pi\chi(x,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\lambda$. Otherwise, $\operatorname{sp}_t(\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\{\kappa_0,\kappa_1\}$, and by Proposition \ref{p:1+1}, $\pi\chi(x,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\min \kappa_0,\kappa_1$.

Let us prove (3). By (2), each of conditions (a), (b), (c), (d) is equivalent to $\pi\chi(x,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\chi(x,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})$. By Proposition \ref{p:1+2}, the latter equality is equivalent to $x$ being a \wob/-point.

Let us prove (4). The point $x$ is a left jump point if and only if $\operatorname{cf}_r(x,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=1$, that is, by (1), $\operatorname{cf} x^{-1}(0)=\kappa_0=1$. The condition $\operatorname{cf} x^{-1}(0)=1$ is equivalent to $x^{-1}(0)$ having a maximal element. Let $\mu = \max x^{-1}(0)$. Then $x=\ensuremath{\left.x\right|_{\mu}} \mathbin{{}^\frown} 0 \mathbin{{}^\frown} 1_\lambda$, and the right jump point $r=\min \lR(x,X)$ equals $\ensuremath{\left.x\right|_{\mu}} \mathbin{{}^\frown} 1 \mathbin{{}^\frown} 0_\lambda$.

Item (5) follows from (4).
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- proposition-18: body_md -->
\label{p:blex:1+1}
Let $\lambda$ be a regular cardinal.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
$\homg l,0\lambda=\{1_\lambda\}$ and $\homg r,0\lambda=\{0_\lambda\}$;
\item
$\homg l,1\lambda$ is the set of right jump points and $\homg r,1\lambda$ is the set of left jump points; these sets are dense in $\mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$;
\item
if $\kappa\leq \lambda$ is a regular cardinal, then 
\begin{enumerate}
\item
the sets $\homg l,\kappa\lambda$ and $\homg r,\kappa\lambda$ are dense in $\mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$;
\item
the topologies of $\homg l,\kappa\lambda$, $\homg r,\kappa\lambda$ and $\homg lr,\kappa\lambda$ coincide with the order topology with respect to the order inherited from $\mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$; accordingly, the spaces listed are LOTS;
\item
if $X\in\{\homg l,\kappa\lambda,\homg r,\kappa\lambda,\homg lr,\kappa\lambda\}$ and $x\in X$, then $\chi(x,X)=\lambda$ and $\pi\chi(x,X)=\kappa$;
\item
the spaces $\homg l,\kappa\lambda$, $\homg r,\kappa\lambda$ and $\homg lr,\kappa\lambda$ are $P_\kappa$-spaces;
\end{enumerate}
\item
if $\kappa< \lambda$ is a regular cardinal, then 
\begin{enumerate}
\item
the sets $\homg l,\kappa\lambda$ and $\homg r,\kappa\lambda$ are disjoint;
\item
$\homg lr,\kappa\lambda=\bbsetx\in\mathbf{2}^{\lambda}: \pi\chi(x,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\kappa\eeset$.
\end{enumerate}
\item
the family
\begin{gather*}
\{ \homg l,0\lambda, \homg r,0\lambda, \homg l,1\lambda, \homg r,1\lambda, {\mathfrak{D}(\lambda)} \} \cup 
\\
\bbset\homg l,\kappa\lambda, \homg r,\kappa\lambda: \kappa<\lambda\text{ is a regular cardinal}\eeset
\end{gather*}
is a partition of $\mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$;
\item
if $\kappa>\omega$ is a regular ordinal, then compact subsets of $\homg l,\kappa\lambda$, $\homg r,\kappa\lambda$ and $\homg lr,\kappa\lambda$ are finite;
\item
the space $\homg lr,\omega\lambda$ is countably compact;
\item
the transfinite line $\omega_1+1$ embeds in the space $\homg lr,\omega{\omega_1}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-18 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Items (1) and (2) follow from Proposition \ref{p:blex:1} (1) and (2).


Let us prove (3). Let us prove (3)(a). Let $U$ be a nonempty open subset of $\mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$. By Proposition \ref{p:1+6}, there exist $a,b\in \mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$ such that $\ilcc[a,b]\subset U$ is a nonempty open subset of $\mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$, $a$ is the minimum of $\mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$ or a right jump point, and $b$ is the maximum of $\mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$ or a left jump point. By Proposition \ref{p:blex:1}(1), $\operatorname{cf}_r(a,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\operatorname{cf}_l(b,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\lambda$. Let $(x_\alpha)_{\alpha<\lambda}\subset \ilcc[a,b]$ be a strictly increasing sequence converging to the point $b$. Let $y$ be the limit of the sequence $(x_\alpha)_{\alpha<\kappa}$. Then $y\in \ilcc[a,b] \cap \homg l,\kappa\lambda\subset U$. Similarly, $\homg r,\kappa\lambda\cap U\neq\varnothing$.

Let us prove (3)(b). The sets $\homg l,\kappa\lambda$ and $\homg r,\kappa\lambda$ are dense in $\mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$ and contain no jump points and no minimum or maximum. Then (b) follows from Proposition \ref{p:1+0a}.

Item (3)(c) follows from Proposition \ref{p:blex:1} (1) and (2).

Let us prove (3)(d). By Proposition \ref{p:1+1} and item (4)(c), $P(x,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\kappa$ for all $x\in \homg lr,\kappa\lambda$. Hence $\homg lr,\kappa\lambda$ is a $P_\kappa$-space.


Let us prove (4). Item (4)(a) follows from $\kappa<\lambda$ and Proposition \ref{p:blex:1} (1) and (2).
Item (4)(b) follows from $\kappa<\lambda$, Proposition \ref{p:blex:1} (1), (2), and Proposition \ref{p:1+1}.

Item (5) follows from the previous items.

Let us prove (6). By (3)(d), $\mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$ is a $P$-space. Hence compact subsets of $\homg lr,\kappa\lambda$ are finite.

Let us prove (7). Let $M\subset \homg lr,\omega\lambda$ and $|M|=\omega$. Let $F$ be the closure of $M$ in $\mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$. Let us show that $F\subset \homg lr,\omega\lambda$. Let $x\in F\setminus M$. Then $wt(x,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\omega$. By Proposition \ref{p:1+1}, $\pi\chi(x,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\omega$. By (5)(b), $x\in \homg lr,\omega\lambda$. Thus $F\subset \homg lr,\omega\lambda$.
                                                                                           

Let us prove (8). Let $r\in \homg r,\omega{\omega_1}$. Take a strictly increasing sequence $(x_\alpha)_{\alpha<\omega_1}\subset \homg l,\omega{\omega_1}$ converging to $r$. Let $F$ be the closure of $(x_\alpha)_{\alpha<\omega_1}$ in $\mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$. Then $F\subset \homg lr,\omega{\omega_1}$ and $F$ is homeomorphic to $\omega_1+1$.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- proposition-19: body_md -->
\label{p:blex:2-1}
Let $f: X\to Y$ be a surjective increasing map between LOTS $X$ and $Y$.
If $f^{-1}(y)$ is a closed interval in $X$ for every $y\in Y$, then $f$ is continuous.
<!-- end proposition-19 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
It suffices to show that $f^{-1}(\lL(y,-\infty))$ and $f^{-1}(\lR(y,+\infty))$ are open for every $y\in Y$.
Let $\ilcc[u,v]=f^{-1}(y)$. Then $f^{-1}(\lL(y,-\infty))=\lL(u,-\infty)$ and $f^{-1}(\lR(y,-\infty))=\lR(v,+\infty)$.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- proposition-20: body_md -->
\label{p:blex:2}
Let $\kappa\leq \lambda$ be ordinals. The projection $\pi^\lambda_\kappa: \mathbf{2}^{\lambda} \to \mathbf{2}^\kappa$ is continuous.
<!-- end proposition-20 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{t:blex:t1}
Let $X$ be a zero-dimensional compact LOTS, $\lambda$ a regular cardinal.
The following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item
$X$ and $\mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$ are order isomorphic;
\item
$X$ and $\mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$ are homeomorphic;
      
                                                                                                                                         
\item
$\chi(x,X)=\lambda$ for all $x\in X$ and $X$ embeds in a product $\prod_{\alpha<\lambda}X_\alpha$ of spaces such that $\chi(X_\alpha)<\lambda$ for $\alpha<\lambda$;
\item
$\chi(x,X)=\lambda$ for all $x\in X$ and the set $M$ of jump points of the LOTS $X$ decomposes into a union $M=\bigcup_{\alpha<\lambda} M_\alpha$ of subsets such that $\chi(\overline{M_\alpha})<\lambda$ for $\alpha<\lambda$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
(1) $\Rightarrow$ (2). Obvious.

(2) $\Rightarrow$ (3). By Proposition \ref{p:blex:2}, $\mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$ embeds via the map $\operatornamewithlimits{ 
  \mathchoice{\vcenter{\hbox{\huge $\bigtriangleup$}}}
             {\vcenter{\hbox{\Large $\bigtriangleup$}}}
             {\mathrm{\bigtriangleup}}
             {\mathrm{\bigtriangleup}}}_{\alpha<\lambda} \pi_\alpha^\lambda$ into the product $\prod_{\alpha<\lambda} \mathbf{2}^{\alpha}$. It remains to note that $\chi(\mathbf{2}^{\alpha})\leq |\alpha|<\lambda$ for $\alpha<\lambda$.

(3) $\Rightarrow$ (4). Assume $X\subset \prod_{\alpha<\lambda}X_\alpha$. We may assume that each $X_\alpha$ is compact. Denote $P_\beta = \prod_{\alpha<\beta}X_\alpha$ for $\beta\leq\lambda$ and let $p_\beta$ be the projection from $P_\lambda$ onto $P_\beta$ for $\beta<\lambda$.

Let $\beta<\lambda$. Since $\lambda$ is a regular cardinal and $\chi(X_\alpha)<\lambda$ for $\lambda<\beta$, we have $\kappa'=\sup\{ \chi(X_\alpha) : \alpha < \beta \}<\lambda$. Set $\kappa=\kappa' + |\beta|$. Then $\chi(P_\beta)\leq\kappa<\lambda$.

For $(a,b)\in\mathfrak{J}(X)$ set
\[
\theta_{a,b}=\min \bbset\alpha<\lambda: p_\alpha(\ilpc(-\infty,a]) \cap  p_\alpha(\ilcp[b,+\infty))=\varnothing\eeset.
\]
Set $M_\beta=\bbseta,b : (a,b)\in\mathfrak{J}(X),\ \theta_{a,b}=\beta\eeset$ for $\beta<\lambda$. Then $M=\bigcup_{\beta<\lambda} M_\beta$. Let us show that $\chi(\overline{M_\beta})<\lambda$. Suppose otherwise. Then $\chi(x,\overline{M_\beta})=\lambda$ for some $x\in \overline{M_\beta}$. Let $L=\ilpp(-\infty,x)\cap M_\beta$ and $R=\ilpp(x,+\infty)\cap M_\beta$. Then $\chi(x,\overline{L})=\lambda$ or $\chi(x,\overline{R})=\lambda$. Assume, without loss of generality, that $\chi(x,\overline{R})=\lambda$. Let $\kappa=\chi(p_\beta(x), P_\beta)$ and $F=p_\beta^{-1}(p_\beta(x))$. Since $\chi(x,\overline{R})=\lambda$, $F$ is a set of type $G_\kappa$ and $\kappa<\lambda$, there is $y>x$ with $\ilpp(x,y)\subset F$, and the set $\ilpp(x,y)\cap M_\beta$ is infinite. There is $(a,b)\in\mathfrak{J}(X)$ with $\{a,b\}\subset \ilpp(x,y)\cap M_\beta$. Then $\{a,b\}\subset F$, and hence $p_\beta(a)=p_\beta(b)=x$, contradicting $p_\beta(\ilpc(-\infty,a]) \cap  p_\beta(\ilcp[b,+\infty))=\varnothing$.

(4) $\Rightarrow$ (1). Set ${\mathcal M}_\alpha=\bbset(a,b)\in \mathfrak{J}(X): \{a,b\}\cap M_\alpha\neq\varnothing\eeset$ for $\alpha<\lambda$ and define the map
\[
\Omega: \mathfrak{J}(X) \to \lambda,\ (a,b) \mapsto \min\bbset\alpha<\lambda: (a,b)\in {\mathcal M}_\alpha\eeset.
\]
Set $\theta_{u,v}=\min  \Omega(\mathfrak{J}(\ilcc[u,v]))$ and ${\mathcal J}_{u,v}=\Omega^{-1}(\theta_{u,v})\cap \mathfrak{J}(\ilcc[u,v])$ for $u,v\in X$, $u<v$. Fix $(a_{u,v},b_{u,v})\in {\mathcal J}_{u,v}$ for every $u,v\in X$, $u<v$.

By induction on $\alpha<\lambda$, we construct increasing continuous maps $f_\alpha: X\to \mathbf{2}^\alpha$ such that the following conditions hold:
\begin{enumerate}
\item
$f_\alpha=\pi_\alpha^\beta\circ f_\beta$, where $\alpha<\beta<\lambda$ and $\pi_\alpha^\beta: \mathbf{2}^\beta\to \mathbf{2}^\alpha$ is the projection;
                                             
\item
if $\alpha<\lambda$, 
$s\in \mathbf{2}^\alpha$ and $\ilcc[u,v]=f^{-1}_\alpha(s)$, then $f^{-1}_{\alpha+1}(s{}^\frown 0)=\ilcc[u,a_{u,v}]$ and $f^{-1}_{\alpha+1}(s{}^\frown 1)=\ilcc[b_{u,v},v]$.
\end{enumerate}
Base of the induction, $\alpha=0$. Then $\mathbf{2}^\alpha=\{\varnothing\}$; let $f_\alpha: X\to \{\varnothing\}$ be the identity map.

Inductive step, $0<\alpha<\lambda$. Consider the case when $\alpha$ is a limit ordinal. For $x\in X$ define $f_\alpha(x)\in \mathbf{2}^\alpha$: $f_\alpha(x)(\beta)=f_{\beta+1}(x)(\beta)$ for $\beta<\alpha$. Consider the case when $\alpha$ is a non-limit ordinal, $\alpha=\beta+1$.
Define the map $g_\alpha: X\to \mathbf{2}$. Let $x\in X$. Since $\chi(x,X)=\lambda$ and $\chi(\mathbf{2}^\alpha)<\lambda$, we have $u<v$, where $\ilcc[u,v]=f^{-1}_\beta(f_\beta(x))$. Set
\[
g_\alpha(x) = \begin{cases}
0,&	x\in \ilcc[u,a_{u,v}],
\\
1,&	x\in \ilcc[b_{u,v},v].
\end{cases}
\]
Define $f_\alpha(x)\in \mathbf{2}^\alpha$:
\[
f_\alpha(x)(\kappa) = \begin{cases}
f_\beta(x)(\kappa),&	\kappa<\beta,
\\
g_\alpha(x),&	\kappa=\beta.
\end{cases}
\]
The maps $f_\alpha$ for $\alpha<\lambda$ have been constructed.

Define the map $f: X\to \mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$. For $x\in X$ set $f(x)(\alpha)=f_{\alpha+1}(x)(\alpha)$.
Since each $f_\alpha$ is a monotone map, $f$ is a monotone map.

For $s\in \mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$ and $\alpha<\lambda$ denote 
\begin{align*}
\ilcc[u_\alpha^s,v_\alpha^s]&=f^{-1}_\alpha(\pi_\alpha^\lambda(s)), 
&
(a_\alpha^s,b_\alpha^s)&=(a_{u_\alpha^s,v_\alpha^s},b_{u_\alpha^s,v_\alpha^s}).
\end{align*}
Then
\begin{align*}
\ilcc[u_{\beta+1}^s,v_{\beta+1}^s] &=
\begin{cases}
\ilcc[u_{\beta}^s,a_{\beta}^s], &  s(\beta)=0,
\\
\ilcc[b_{\beta}^s,v_{\beta}^s], &  s(\beta)=1,
\end{cases}
\\
\ilcc[u_{\gamma}^s,v_{\gamma}^s] &= \bigcap_{\alpha<\gamma}\ilcc[u_\alpha^s,v_\alpha^s],
\end{align*}
for $\beta<\lambda$ and limit $\gamma<\lambda$. Hence 
\[
f^{-1}(s) = \ilcc[u^s,v^s]=\bigcap_{\alpha<\lambda}\ilcc[u_\alpha^s,v_\alpha^s]\neq\varnothing.
\]
Since $f^{-1}(s)\neq\varnothing$ for all $s\in\mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$, $f$ is surjective.
Since $f$ is a monotone surjection and $f^{-1}(s)$ is a closed interval for all $s\in\mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$, Proposition \ref{p:blex:2-1} implies that $f$ is continuous.

Let us show that $f$ is a homeomorphism; for this it suffices to check that $f$ is injective. Suppose otherwise. Then $|f^{-1}(s)|>1$, and hence $u^s<v^s$ for some $s\in\mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$.
 
Denote $\theta^s=\theta_{u^s,v^s}$ and $\theta_\alpha=\theta_{u_\alpha^s,v_\alpha^s}$ for $\alpha<\lambda$.
Then
\[
\ilcc[u^s,v^s] \subsetneq \ilcc[u^s_\beta,v^s_\beta] \subsetneq \ilcc[u^s_\alpha,v^s_\alpha]
\qquad\text{ and } \qquad \theta_\alpha\leq \theta_\beta\leq  \theta^s < \lambda
\]
for $\alpha< \beta < \lambda$. 
Hence either $u^s_\alpha<u^s$ for all $\alpha<\lambda$, or $v^s<v^s_\alpha$ for all $\alpha<\lambda$. Assume, without loss of generality, that $u^s_\alpha<u^s$ for all $\alpha<\lambda$.
Since $\lambda$ is a regular cardinal and the sequence $(\theta_\alpha)_{\alpha<\lambda}$ is bounded and increasing, the sequence $(\theta_\alpha)_{\alpha<\lambda}$ stabilizes: for some $\theta<\lambda$ and $\alpha_0<\lambda$, $\theta_\alpha=\theta$ for all $\alpha$ with $\alpha_0\leq \alpha < \lambda$. Set
\[
C=\bbset \alpha<\lambda: \alpha_0<\alpha,\ u^s_{\alpha_0} < u^s_{\alpha} < u^s_{\alpha+1} \eeset
\]
Then $|C|=\lambda$, $u^s_{\alpha} < a^s_\alpha< b^s_\alpha=u^s_{\alpha+1}$, and $(a^s_\alpha,b^s_\alpha)\in {\mathcal M}_\theta$ for $\alpha\in C$.
Set $A=\bbseta^s_\alpha:\alpha\in C\eeset$, $B=\bbsetb^s_\alpha:\alpha\in C\eeset$, and $S=M_\theta\cap(A\cup B)$. Since $\{a^s_\alpha,b^s_\alpha\}\cap M_\theta\neq\varnothing$ for $\alpha\in C$, we get $u^s\in \overline{S}$ and $\chi(u^s,\overline{S})=\lambda$. Hence $u^s\in \overline{M_\theta}$ and $\chi(u^s,\overline{M_\theta})=\lambda$, contradicting $\chi(\overline{M_\theta})<\lambda$.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- proposition-21: body_md -->
\label{p:blex:ct1}
Let $\lambda$ be a regular cardinal, $X$ a closed subset of $\mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$.
The following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item
$X$ and $\mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$ are order isomorphic;
\item
$\chi(x,X)=\lambda$ for all $x\in X$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-21 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
(1) $\Rightarrow$ (2) follows from Theorem \ref{t:blex:t1}.
Let us prove (2) $\Rightarrow$ (1). Since, by Theorem \ref{t:blex:t1}, condition (3) of Theorem \ref{t:blex:t1} holds for $\mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$ and $X\subset \mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$, condition (3) of Theorem \ref{t:blex:t1} holds for $X$.
Hence $X$ and $\mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$ are order isomorphic.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- proposition-22: body_md -->
\label{p:blex:3-1}
Let $X$ be a compact zero-dimensional LOTS. Then $w(X)=|\mathfrak{J}(X)|$.
<!-- end proposition-22 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Since $X$ is a compact zero-dimensional LOTS, ${\mathcal U}=\bbset\ilpp(-\infty,a), \ilpp(b,+\infty): (a,b)\in \mathfrak{J}(X)\eeset$ forms a clopen subbase of the zero-dimensional compact space $X$. Hence $w(X)=|\mathfrak{J}(X)|$.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- proposition-23: body_md -->
\label{p:blex:3}
Let $\lambda$ be a limit ordinal. Then $w(\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=c(\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\sup\bbset2^\alpha: \alpha<\lambda\eeset$.
<!-- end proposition-23 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
By Proposition \ref{p:blex:2}, $\mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$ embeds via the map $\operatornamewithlimits{ 
  \mathchoice{\vcenter{\hbox{\huge $\bigtriangleup$}}}
             {\vcenter{\hbox{\Large $\bigtriangleup$}}}
             {\mathrm{\bigtriangleup}}
             {\mathrm{\bigtriangleup}}}_{\alpha<\lambda} \pi_\alpha^\lambda$ into the product $\prod_{\alpha<\lambda} \mathbf{2}^{\alpha}$. Hence $w(\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})\leq \tau= \sup\bbset2^\alpha: \alpha<\lambda\eeset$.
For $\alpha<\lambda$, under the map $\pi^\lambda_\alpha$ the preimage of each point has nonempty interior. Hence $c(\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})\geq \tau$. It remains to note that $c(\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})\leq w(\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})$.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{t:blex:1}
Let $\lambda$ be a regular cardinal, $X$ a compact zero-dimensional LOTS with $w(X)=\lambda$.
The following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item
$X$ and $\mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$ are order isomorphic;
\item
$\chi(x,X)=\lambda$ for all $x\in X$.
\end{enumerate}
If either of these conditions holds, then $\lambda=\sup\bbset2^\alpha: \alpha<\lambda\eeset$.
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
By Proposition \ref{p:blex:3}, (1) implies $\lambda=\sup\bbset2^\alpha: \alpha<\lambda\eeset$.
(1) $\Rightarrow$ (2) follows from Theorem \ref{t:blex:t1}.
Let us prove (2) $\Rightarrow$ (1). Since $w(X)=\lambda$, $X$ embeds in $[0,1]^\lambda$, so condition (3) of Theorem \ref{t:blex:t1} holds for $X$. Hence $X$ and $\mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$ are order isomorphic.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- cor-3: body_md -->
\label{c:blex:1}
{\rm ($\mathrm{CH}$)}
Let $X$ be a compact zero-dimensional LOTS.
The following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item
the LOTS $X$ is order isomorphic to $\mathbf{2}^{\omega_1}$;
\item
$w(X)=\omega_1$ and $\chi(x,X)=\omega_1$ for all $x\in X$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end cor-3 -->
<!-- proposition-24: body_md -->
\label{p:blex:5}
                      
$\mathbf{2}^{\omega_1}$ does not embed homeomorphically in a homogeneous GO space.
<!-- end proposition-24 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
Suppose $\mathbf{2}^{\omega_1}$ embeds homeomorphically in a homogeneous GO space $X$, with $X\subset Y$ where $Y$ is a LOTS. Let $K\subset X$ be a compact subset homeomorphic to $\mathbf{2}^{\omega_1}$.
By Theorem \ref{t:blex:t1}, $K$ is order isomorphic to $\mathbf{2}^{\omega_1}$. Then $\operatorname{cf}_l(x,K)=\operatorname{cf}_r(x,K)=\omega_1$ for some $x\in K$. Hence $\operatorname{cf}_l(x,X)=\operatorname{cf}_r(x,X)=\omega_1$. By Proposition \ref{p:1+0}, $x$ is a WOB-point in $X$ and $\chi(x,X)=\omega_1$. Hence $x$ is a $P$-point in $X$. By homogeneity of $X$, $X$ is a $P$-space, contradicting the fact that compact subsets of $P$-spaces are finite.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{t:blex:2}
Let $\lambda$ be a regular cardinal, $a,b\in \mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$, $a<b$.
The following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item
the LOTS $\ilcc[a,b]$ and $\mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$ are order isomorphic;
\item
$\operatorname{cf}_r(a,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\operatorname{cf}_l(b,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\lambda$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
The points $a$ and $b$ are not isolated in $\ilcc[a,b]$, so Proposition \ref{p:1+1.5} gives $\chi(a,\ilcc[a,b])=\operatorname{cf}_r(a,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})$. For $x\in \ilpp(a,b)$, $\chi(x,\ilcc[a,b])=\chi(x,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\lambda$.
Hence condition (2) is equivalent to $\chi(x,\ilcc[a,b])=\lambda$ for $x\in \ilcc[a,b]$.
Then (1) $\Leftrightarrow$ (2) follows from Proposition \ref{p:blex:ct1}.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{t:blex:3}
Let $\lambda$ be a regular cardinal, $a,b,c,d\in \mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$, $a<b$ and $c<d$.
The following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item
the LOTS $\ilcc[a,b]$ and $\ilcc[c,d]$ are order isomorphic and have no isolated points;
\item
$\operatorname{cf}_r(a,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\operatorname{cf}_r(c,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})\geq \omega$ and
$\operatorname{cf}_l(b,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\operatorname{cf}_l(d,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})\geq \omega$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
Let 
$\alpha=\operatorname{cf}_r(a,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\operatorname{cf}_r(c,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})$ and
$\beta = \operatorname{cf}_l(b,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\operatorname{cf}_l(d,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})$.

Clearly, (1) $\Rightarrow$ (2). Let us prove (2) $\Rightarrow$ (1).
Take $(a',b'),(c',d')\in \mathfrak{J}(\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})$ such that $a< a'<b'< b$ and $c< c'<d'< d$.
By Proposition \ref{p:blex:1}, $\operatorname{cf}_l(a',\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\operatorname{cf}_r(b',\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\operatorname{cf}_l(c',\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\operatorname{cf}_r(d',\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\lambda$. Since $\ilcc[a,b]=\ilcc[a,a']\cup \ilcc[b',b]$ and $\ilcc[c,d]=\ilcc[c,c']\cup \ilcc[d',d]$, it suffices to prove that $\ilcc[a,a']$ is order isomorphic to $\ilcc[c,c']$ and $\ilcc[b',b]$ is order isomorphic to $\ilcc[d',d]$. This fact follows from the theorem being proved in the case $\alpha=\lambda$ or $\beta=\lambda$. Let us prove (2) $\Rightarrow$ (1) in the case $\alpha=\lambda$. The set $M=\bbsetx\in\mathbf{2}^{\lambda}: \pi\chi(x,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\lambda\eeset$ is dense in $\mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$. Take strictly increasing sequences $(x_\theta)_{\theta<\beta}$ and $(y_\theta)_{\theta<\beta}$ in $\mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$ with $x_0=a$, $y_0=c$, $x_\theta,y_\theta\in M$ for $\theta>0$, $(x_\theta)_{\theta<\beta}$ cofinal in $\ilcp[a,b)$, and $(y_\theta)_{\theta<\beta}$ cofinal in $\ilcp[c,d)$. Then $\operatorname{cf}_r(x_\theta,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\operatorname{cf}_l(x_{\theta+1},\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\operatorname{cf}_r(y_\theta,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\operatorname{cf}_l(y_{\theta+1},\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\lambda$ for $\theta<\beta$. By Theorem \ref{t:blex:2} there is an order isomorphism $f_\theta: \ilcc[x_\theta,x_{\theta+1}]\to \ilcc[y_\theta,y_{\theta+1}]$ for $\theta<\beta$. Define an order isomorphism $f: \ilcc[a,b]\to \ilcc[c,d]$:
\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}
y_\theta, & \text{if }x=x_\theta\text{ for some }\theta<\beta,
\\
f_\theta(x), & \text{if }x\in \ilpp(x_\theta,x_{\theta+1})\text{ for some }\theta<\beta,
\\
d, & \text{if }x=b
\end{cases}
\]
for $x\in \ilcc[a,b]$.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- proposition-25: body_md -->
\label{p:blexhome:1-1}
Let $\lambda$ be a regular cardinal and $x,y\in \mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$.
The following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item
$f(x)=y$ for some $f\in\mathcal{H}_{+}(\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})$;
\item
$\operatorname{cf}_r(x,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\operatorname{cf}_r(y,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})$ and
$\operatorname{cf}_l(x,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\operatorname{cf}_l(y,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-25 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
Let 
$\alpha=\operatorname{cf}_r(x,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\operatorname{cf}_r(y,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})$ and
$\beta = \operatorname{cf}_l(x,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\operatorname{cf}_l(y,\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})$.
By Proposition \ref{p:blex:1}, $\lambda\in\{\alpha,\beta\}$.
Clearly, (1) $\Rightarrow$ (2). Let us prove (2) $\Rightarrow$ (1).
If $0\in\{\alpha,\beta\}$, then $x=y$ and the statement is obvious.

Consider the case $1\in\{\alpha,\beta\}$. Consider the case $\alpha=1$. Then $x$ and $y$ are right jump points and $\beta=\lambda$. Let $x'$ and $y'$ be the corresponding left jump points. Then $\operatorname{cf}_r(0_\lambda)=\operatorname{cf}_l(x')=\operatorname{cf}_r(x)=\operatorname{cf}_l(y')=\operatorname{cf}_r(y)=\operatorname{cf}_l(1_\lambda)=\lambda$. By Theorem \ref{t:blex:3} there exist order isomorphisms $f_1: \ilcc[0_\lambda,x']\to \ilcc[0_\lambda,y']$ and $f_2: \ilcc[x,1_\lambda]\to \ilcc[y,1_\lambda]$. For $u\in \mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$, set
\[
f(u)=\begin{cases}
f_1(u), & u \leq x',
\\
f_2(u), & u \geq x.
\end{cases}
\]
Then $f\in\mathcal{H}_{+}(\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})$ and $f(x)=y$.
Consider the case $\beta=1$. Then $\operatorname{cf}_l(R_\lambda(x),\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\operatorname{cf}_l(R_\lambda(y),\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=1$ and $\operatorname{cf}_r(R_\lambda(x),\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\operatorname{cf}_r(R_\lambda(y),\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\lambda$. Hence $f'(R_\lambda(x))=R_\lambda(y)$ for some $f'\in \mathcal{H}_{+}(\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})$. We obtain $f(x)=y$ for $f=R_\lambda\circ f' \circ R_\lambda\in \mathcal{H}_{+}(\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})$.

Consider the case when $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are infinite cardinals.
Since $0_\lambda<x<1_\lambda$, $0_\lambda<y<1_\lambda$, $\alpha\geq \omega$, and $\beta\geq \omega$, Theorem \ref{t:blex:3} gives order isomorphisms $f_1: \ilcc[0_\lambda,x]\to \ilcc[0_\lambda,y]$ and $f_2: \ilcc[x,1_\lambda]\to \ilcc[y,1_\lambda]$. For $u\in \mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$, set
\[
f(u)=\begin{cases}
f_1(u), & u < x,
\\
y, & u=x,
\\
f_2(u), & u > x.
\end{cases}
\]
Then $f\in\mathcal{H}_{+}(\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})$ and $f(x)=y$.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- proposition-26: body_md -->
\label{p:blexhome:1}
Let $\lambda$ be a regular cardinal and $\kappa\leq\lambda$ a cardinal.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
If $x,y\in \homg l,\kappa\lambda$ or $x,y\in \homg r,\kappa\lambda$, then there is $f\in\mathcal{H}_{+}(X)$ with $f(x)=y$.
\item
If $x\in \homg l,\kappa\lambda$, $y\in \homg r,\kappa\lambda$, or $x\in \homg r,\kappa\lambda$, $y\in \homg l,\kappa\lambda$, then there is $f\in\mathcal{H}_{-}(X)$ with $f(x)=y$.
\item
If $x,y\in \homg lr,\kappa\lambda$, then there is $f\in\mathcal{H}_{\pm}(X)$ with $f(x)=y$ and $f(\homg lr,\kappa\lambda)=\homg lr,\kappa\lambda$.
\item
if $f\in\mathcal{H}_{+}(X)$, then $f(\homg l,\kappa\lambda)=\homg l,\kappa\lambda$, $f(\homg r,\kappa\lambda)=\homg r,\kappa\lambda$, and $f(\homg lr,\kappa\lambda)=\homg lr,\kappa\lambda$;
\item
$R_\lambda(\homg l,\kappa\lambda)=\homg r,\kappa\lambda$, $R_\lambda(\homg r,\kappa\lambda)=\homg l,\kappa\lambda$, and $R_\lambda(\homg lr,\kappa\lambda)=\homg lr,\kappa\lambda$;
\item
if $f\in\mathcal{H}_{-}(X)$, then $f(\homg l,\kappa\lambda)=\homg r,\kappa\lambda$, $f(\homg r,\kappa\lambda)=\homg l,\kappa\lambda$, and $f(\homg lr,\kappa\lambda)=\homg lr,\kappa\lambda$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-26 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
Items (4), (5) and (6) are obvious. Item (1) follows from Proposition \ref{p:blexhome:1-1}.

Let us prove (2). Let $x'=R_\lambda(x)$. By (1), there is $f'\in\mathcal{H}_{+}(\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})$ with $f'(x')=y$. Let $f = f' \circ R_\lambda$. Then $f\in\mathcal{H}_{-}(\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})$ and $f(x)=y$.

Let us prove (3). If $x,y\in \homg l,\kappa\lambda$ or $x,y\in \homg r,\kappa\lambda$, then (3) follows from (1) and (4).
If $x\in \homg l,\kappa\lambda$, $y\in \homg r,\kappa\lambda$, or $x\in \homg r,\kappa\lambda$, $y\in \homg l,\kappa\lambda$, then (3) follows from (2) and (6).
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- proposition-27: body_md -->
\label{p:blexhome:2}
Let $\lambda$ be a regular cardinal.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
The family
\begin{gather*}
\{ \homg l,0\lambda, \homg r,0\lambda, \homg l,1\lambda, \homg r,1\lambda, {\mathfrak{D}(\lambda)} \} \cup 
\\
\bbset\homg l,\kappa\lambda, \homg r,\kappa\lambda: \kappa<\lambda\text{ is a regular cardinal}\eeset
\end{gather*}
is the family of orbits of the action of the group $\mathcal{H}_{+}(\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})$ on $\mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$.
\item
The family
\begin{gather*}
\{ \homg lr,0\lambda,  \homg lr,1\lambda, {\mathfrak{D}(\lambda)} \} \cup 
\\
\bbset\homg lr,\kappa\lambda: \kappa<\lambda\text{ is a regular cardinal}\eeset
\end{gather*}
is the family of orbits of the action of the group $\mathcal{H}_{\pm}(\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})$ on $\mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-27 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
\label{t:blexhome:1}
Let $\kappa\leq\lambda$ be regular cardinals. The spaces $\homg l,\kappa\lambda$, $\homg r,\kappa\lambda$ are order-homogeneous LOTS. The space $\homg lr,\kappa\lambda$ is a $\pm$-order-homogeneous LOTS.
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
By Proposition \ref{p:blex:1+1}(3)(b), the spaces $\homg l,\kappa\lambda$, $\homg r,\kappa\lambda$ and $\homg r,\kappa\lambda$ are LOTS with the order inherited from $\mathbf{2}^{\lambda}$. By Proposition \ref{p:blexhome:2}(1), the LOTS $\homg l,\kappa\lambda$ and $\homg r,\kappa\lambda$ are order-homogeneous. By Proposition \ref{p:blexhome:2}(2), the LOTS $\homg lr,\kappa\lambda$ is $\pm$-order-homogeneous.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- cor-4: body_md -->
\label{c:blexhome:1}
Let $\kappa\leq\lambda$ be regular cardinals. The spaces $\homg l,\kappa\lambda$, $\homg r,\kappa\lambda$ and $\homg lr,\kappa\lambda$ are homogeneous LOTS.
<!-- end cor-4 -->
<!-- proposition-28: body_md -->
\label{p:exos:1}
Let $X$ be a compact LOTS, $L$ and $R$ locally compact LOTS, $L$ having a minimum and no maximum, and $R$ having a maximum and no minimum. Then $X$ embeds in $\mathcal{E}(X,L,R)$, $\mathcal{E}(X,L,R)$ is compact, and $\mathcal{E}_\omega(X,L,R)$ is $\sigma$-compact.
<!-- end proposition-28 -->
<!-- statement-1: body_md -->
\label{s:exos:1}
Let $M\subset {\mathcal B}_*(X)$.
Then $\mathcal{E}_\omega(\mathcal{E}(X;M))=\mathcal{E}_\omega(X)$.
<!-- end statement-1 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
By induction on $n\in\omega$ we define sets $M_n\subset {\mathcal B}_*(X_n)$, where $X_n=\mathcal{E}_n(X)$.
Set $M_0=M$. Set $M_{n+1}={\mathcal B}_*({\mathcal D}_{M_n}(X_n))$ for $n>0$. Set $Z_n=\mathcal{E}(X_n;M_n)$ for ${n\in\omega}$. Then $Z_0=\mathcal{E}(X;M)$, $Z_{n+1}=\mathcal{E}(Z_n)$, and $X_n\subset Z_n\subset X_{n+1}$. Hence $\mathcal{E}_\omega(X)=\bigcup_{n\in\omega} X_n=\bigcup_{n\in\omega} Z_n=\mathcal{E}_\omega(Z_0)$.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- statement-2: body_md -->
\label{s:exos:2}
If $R$ is order reversing isomorphic to $L$, then every $f\in\mathcal{H}_{\pm}(X)$ extends to some $\hat f\in \mathcal{H}_{\pm}(\mathcal{E}_\omega(X))$.
<!-- end statement-2 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
Let $\varphi: L\to R$ and $\psi: R\to L$ be order reversing isomorphisms such that $\varphi\circ \psi$ is the identity map of $L$ onto itself.
\begin{claim}\label{cl:exos:1-1}
Let $Y$ be a LOTS. Every $f\in\mathcal{H}_{\pm}(Y)$ extends to some $\hat f\in \mathcal{H}_{\pm}(\mathcal{E}(Y))$.
\end{claim}
\begin{proof}
Suppose $f\in \mathcal{H}_{+}(Y)$. Set
\[
\hat f(x) = \begin{cases}
f(x), & x\in Y,
\\
(f(y),z), & x=(y,z)\in {\mathcal D}(Y).
\end{cases}
\]
Then $\hat f\in \mathcal{H}_{+}(\mathcal{E}(Y))$.

Suppose $f\in \mathcal{H}_{-}(Y)$. Set
\[
\hat f(x) = \begin{cases}
f(x), & x\in Y,
\\
(f(y),\varphi(z)), & x=(y,z)\in {\mathcal B}_r(Y) \times L,
\\
(f(y),\psi(z)), & x=(y,z)\in {\mathcal B}_l(Y) \times R.
\end{cases}
\]
Then $\hat f\in \mathcal{H}_{-}(\mathcal{E}(Y))$.
\end{proof}
By Fact \ref{cl:exos:1-1}, there exist $f_n\in\mathcal{H}_{\pm}(\mathcal{E}_n(X))$ for ${n\in\omega}$ such that $f_0=f$ and $f_n=\ensuremath{\left.f_{n+1}\right|_{\mathcal{E}_n(X)}}$ for ${n\in\omega}$. Define $\hat f: \mathcal{E}_\omega(X)\to \mathcal{E}_\omega(X)$ by $\hat f(x)=f(x)$ for $x\in X$, and $\hat f(x)=f_n(x)$ for $x\in \mathcal{E}_n(X)\setminus \mathcal{E}_{n-1}(X)$.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- claim-1: body_md -->
\label{cl:exos:1-1}
Let $Y$ be a LOTS. Every $f\in\mathcal{H}_{\pm}(Y)$ extends to some $\hat f\in \mathcal{H}_{\pm}(\mathcal{E}(Y))$.
<!-- end claim-1 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
Suppose $f\in \mathcal{H}_{+}(Y)$. Set
\[
\hat f(x) = \begin{cases}
f(x), & x\in Y,
\\
(f(y),z), & x=(y,z)\in {\mathcal D}(Y).
\end{cases}
\]
Then $\hat f\in \mathcal{H}_{+}(\mathcal{E}(Y))$.

Suppose $f\in \mathcal{H}_{-}(Y)$. Set
\[
\hat f(x) = \begin{cases}
f(x), & x\in Y,
\\
(f(y),\varphi(z)), & x=(y,z)\in {\mathcal B}_r(Y) \times L,
\\
(f(y),\psi(z)), & x=(y,z)\in {\mathcal B}_l(Y) \times R.
\end{cases}
\]
Then $\hat f\in \mathcal{H}_{-}(\mathcal{E}(Y))$.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- theorem-13: body_md -->
\label{t:exos:1}
Let $X$, $L$ and $R$ be LOTS.
Let $L$ have a minimum and no maximum, and let $L$ and $\operatorname{rev} R$ be order isomorphic.
Suppose the following conditions hold:
\begin{enumerate}
\item
if $x,y\in X\setminus {\mathcal B}_*(X)$, then $f(x)=y$ for some $f\in\mathcal{H}_{\pm}(X)$;
\item
the LOTS $\ilpc(-\infty,a] + R + \ilpp(a,+\infty)$ and $\ilpp(-\infty,b) + L + \ilcp[b,+\infty)$ are order isomorphic to $X$ for $a\in {\mathcal B}_l(X)$ and $b\in {\mathcal B}_r(X)$.
\end{enumerate}
Then $\mathcal{E}_\omega(X,L,R)$ is a $\pm$-order-homogeneous LOTS.
<!-- end theorem-13 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
Condition (2) is equivalent to $\mathcal{E}(X;\{x\})$ being order isomorphic to $X$ for $x\in{\mathcal B}_*(X)$.
\begin{claim}\label{cl:exos:1}
Let $u\in \mathcal{E}_\omega(X)$. There is $Y\subset \mathcal{E}_\omega(X)$ such that $X\subset Y$, $\mathcal{E}_\omega(Y)=\mathcal{E}_\omega(X)$, $Y$ is order isomorphic to $X$, and $u\in Y\setminus {\mathcal B}_*(Y)$.
\end{claim}
\begin{proof}
For some $n\in\omega$,
\begin{align*}
u &= (x,u_1,...,u_n)\in \mathcal{E}_n(X).
\end{align*}
Set $x_0=x$, $x_1=(x,u_1)$, ..., $x_n=(x,u_1,...,u_n)=u$. Define $X_i\subset \mathcal{E}_\omega(X)$ for $i=0,1,...,n$ such that $x_i\in X_i$ for $i\leq n$ and $x_i \in {\mathcal B}_*(X_i)$ for $i<n$. Set $X_0=X$ and $X_i=\mathcal{E}(X_{i-1};\{x_{i-1}\})$ for $i>0$. By Statement \ref{s:exos:1}, $\mathcal{E}_\omega(X_i) = \mathcal{E}_\omega(X)$, and by condition (2), $X_i$ is order isomorphic to $X$ for $i=0,1,...,n$. If $u=x_n\notin {\mathcal B}_*(X_n)$, set $Y=X_n$. If $u\in {\mathcal B}_*(X_n)$, set $Y=\mathcal{E}(X_{n};\{u\})$. Then $u\notin {\mathcal B}_*(Y)$. By Statement \ref{s:exos:1} and (2), $Y$ is order isomorphic to $X$ and $\mathcal{E}_\omega(Y)=\mathcal{E}_\omega(X)$.
\end{proof}
Let $x,y\in\mathcal{E}_\omega(X)$. By Fact \ref{cl:exos:1}, there is $Y'\subset \mathcal{E}_\omega(X)$ such that $X\subset Y'$, $x\in Y'\setminus {\mathcal B}_*(Y')$, $\mathcal{E}_\omega(Y')=\mathcal{E}_\omega(X)$, and $Y'$ is order isomorphic to $X$. By Fact \ref{cl:exos:1}, there is $Y\subset \mathcal{E}_\omega(Y')$ such that $Y'\subset Y$, $y\in Y\setminus {\mathcal B}_*(Y)$, $\mathcal{E}_\omega(Y)=\mathcal{E}_\omega(Y')=\mathcal{E}_\omega(X)$, and $Y$ is order isomorphic to $Y'$ and to $X$.

Thus $x,y\in Y\setminus {\mathcal B}_*(Y)$, $\mathcal{E}_\omega(Y)=\mathcal{E}_\omega(X)$, and $Y$ is order isomorphic to $X$.
By condition (1), $f(x)=y$ for some $f\in\mathcal{H}_{\pm}(Y)$. By Statement \ref{cl:exos:1-1}, $f$ extends to some $\hat f\in \mathcal{H}_{\pm}(\mathcal{E}_\omega(Y))$. Then $\hat f(x)=y$ for $\hat f\in \mathcal{H}_{\pm}(\mathcal{E}_\omega(X))$. Hence the LOTS $\mathcal{E}_\omega(X)$ is $\pm$-order-homogeneous.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- claim-2: body_md -->
\label{cl:exos:1}
Let $u\in \mathcal{E}_\omega(X)$. There is $Y\subset \mathcal{E}_\omega(X)$ such that $X\subset Y$, $\mathcal{E}_\omega(Y)=\mathcal{E}_\omega(X)$, $Y$ is order isomorphic to $X$, and $u\in Y\setminus {\mathcal B}_*(Y)$.
<!-- end claim-2 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
For some $n\in\omega$,
\begin{align*}
u &= (x,u_1,...,u_n)\in \mathcal{E}_n(X).
\end{align*}
Set $x_0=x$, $x_1=(x,u_1)$, ..., $x_n=(x,u_1,...,u_n)=u$. Define $X_i\subset \mathcal{E}_\omega(X)$ for $i=0,1,...,n$ such that $x_i\in X_i$ for $i\leq n$ and $x_i \in {\mathcal B}_*(X_i)$ for $i<n$. Set $X_0=X$ and $X_i=\mathcal{E}(X_{i-1};\{x_{i-1}\})$ for $i>0$. By Statement \ref{s:exos:1}, $\mathcal{E}_\omega(X_i) = \mathcal{E}_\omega(X)$, and by condition (2), $X_i$ is order isomorphic to $X$ for $i=0,1,...,n$. If $u=x_n\notin {\mathcal B}_*(X_n)$, set $Y=X_n$. If $u\in {\mathcal B}_*(X_n)$, set $Y=\mathcal{E}(X_{n};\{u\})$. Then $u\notin {\mathcal B}_*(Y)$. By Statement \ref{s:exos:1} and (2), $Y$ is order isomorphic to $X$ and $\mathcal{E}_\omega(Y)=\mathcal{E}_\omega(X)$.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- proposition-29: body_md -->
\label{p:bsc:1-1}
$\chi(x,\mathbf{S})=\omega_1$ for all $x\in \mathbf{S}$, and $w(\mathbf{S})=|\mathbf{S}|=2^{\omega_1}$.
<!-- end proposition-29 -->
<!-- proposition-30: body_md -->
\label{p:bsc:1}
Let $a,b,c,d\in \mathbf{S}$, $a<b$ and $c<d$.
The following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item
the LOTS $\ilcc[a,b]$ and $\ilcc[c,d]$ are order isomorphic and have no isolated points;
\item
$\operatorname{cf}_r(a,\mathbf{S})=\operatorname{cf}_r(c,\mathbf{S})\geq \omega$ and
$\operatorname{cf}_l(b,\mathbf{S})=\operatorname{cf}_l(d,\mathbf{S})\geq \omega$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-30 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
Let
$\alpha=\operatorname{cf}_r(a,\mathbf{S})=\operatorname{cf}_r(c,\mathbf{S})$ and
$\beta = \operatorname{cf}_l(b,\mathbf{S})=\operatorname{cf}_l(d,\mathbf{S})$.
Clearly, (1) $\Rightarrow$ (2). Let us prove (2) $\Rightarrow$ (1). Since $\operatorname{cf}_r(\pi(a),\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\operatorname{cf}_r(\pi(c),\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\alpha$ and
$\operatorname{cf}_l(\pi(b),\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\operatorname{cf}_l(\pi(d),\mathbf{2}^{\lambda})=\beta$, Theorem \ref{t:blex:3} gives an order isomorphism $f': \ilcc[\pi(a),\pi(b)]\to \ilcc[\pi(c),\pi(d)]$. Define an order isomorphism $f: \ilcc[a,b]\to\ilcc[c,d]$ by setting
\[
f(u)=\begin{cases}
f'(u), & u\in {\mathfrak{D}(\omega_1)},
\\
(f'(x),y), & u\notin {\mathfrak{D}(\omega_1)}\text{ and }u=(x,y),
\end{cases}
\]
for $u\in \ilcc[a,b]$.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- proposition-31: body_md -->
\label{p:bsc:1+1}
If $(a,b)\in \mathfrak{J}(\mathbf{S})$, then $\ilcc[0_{\omega_1},a]$ and $\ilcc[b,1_{\omega_1}]$ are order isomorphic to $\mathbf{S}$.
<!-- end proposition-31 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
Since $\operatorname{cf}_r(0_{\omega_1},{\mathcal S})=\operatorname{cf}_l(a,{\mathcal S})=\operatorname{cf}_r(b,{\mathcal S})=\operatorname{cf}_l(1_{\omega_1},{\mathcal S})=\omega_1$, Proposition \ref{p:bsc:1} implies that the LOTS $\ilcc[0_{\omega_1},a]$, $\ilcc[b,1_{\omega_1}]$ and $\mathbf{S}$ are order isomorphic.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- proposition-32: body_md -->
\label{p:bsc:2}
Let $x,y\in \mathbf{S}$.
The following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item
$f(x)=y$ for some $f\in\mathcal{H}_{+}(\mathbf{S})$;
\item
$\operatorname{cf}_r(x,\mathbf{S})=\operatorname{cf}_r(y,\mathbf{S})$ and
$\operatorname{cf}_l(x,\mathbf{S})=\operatorname{cf}_l(y,\mathbf{S})$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-32 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
Let
$\alpha=\operatorname{cf}_r(x,\mathbf{S})=\operatorname{cf}_r(y,\mathbf{S})$ and
$\beta = \operatorname{cf}_l(x,\mathbf{S})=\operatorname{cf}_l(y,\mathbf{S})$.
Clearly, (1) $\Rightarrow$ (2). Let us prove (2) $\Rightarrow$ (1).
If $0\in\{\alpha,\beta\}$, then $x=y$ and the statement is obvious.

Consider the case $1\in\{\alpha,\beta\}$. Consider the case $\alpha=1$. Then $x$ and $y$ are right jump points and $\beta=\omega_1$. Let $x'$ and $y'$ be the corresponding left jump points. By Proposition \ref{p:bsc:1+1}, there exist order isomorphisms $f_1: \ilcc[0_{\omega_1},x']\to \ilcc[0_{\omega_1},y']$ and $f_2: \ilcc[x,1_{\omega_1}]\to \ilcc[y,1_{\omega_1}]$. For $u\in \mathbf{S}$, set
\[
f(u)=\begin{cases}
f_1(u), & u \leq x',
\\
f_2(u), & u \geq x.
\end{cases}
\]
Then $f\in\mathcal{H}_{+}(\mathbf{S})$ and $f(x)=y$.
Consider the case $\beta=1$. Then $\operatorname{cf}_l(\mathbf{R}(x),\mathbf{S})=\operatorname{cf}_l(\mathbf{R}(y),\mathbf{S})=1$ and $\operatorname{cf}_r(\mathbf{R}(x),\mathbf{S})=\operatorname{cf}_r(\mathbf{R}(y),\mathbf{S})=\lambda$. Hence $f'(\mathbf{R}(x))=\mathbf{R}(y)$ for some $f'\in \mathcal{H}_{+}(\mathbf{S})$. We obtain $f(x)=y$ for $f=\mathbf{R}\circ f' \circ \mathbf{R}\in \mathcal{H}_{+}(\mathbf{S})$.

Consider the case when $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are infinite cardinals.
Since $0_{\omega_1}<x<1_{\omega_1}$, $0_{\omega_1}<y<1_{\omega_1}$, $\alpha\geq \omega$, and $\beta\geq \omega$, Proposition \ref{p:bsc:1} gives order isomorphisms $f_1: \ilcc[0_{\omega_1},x]\to \ilcc[0_{\omega_1},y]$ and $f_2: \ilcc[x,1_{\omega_1}]\to \ilcc[y,1_{\omega_1}]$. For $u\in \mathbf{S}$, set
\[
f(u)=\begin{cases}
f_1(u), & u < x,
\\
y, & u=x,
\\
f_2(u), & u > x.
\end{cases}
\]
Then $f\in\mathcal{H}_{+}(\mathbf{S})$ and $f(x)=y$.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- proposition-33: body_md -->
\label{p:bsc:3}
\begin{enumerate}
\item
The family ${\mathcal S}$
is the family of orbits of the action of the group $\mathcal{H}_{+}(\mathbf{S})$ on $\mathbf{S}$.
\item
The family $\widetilde{\mathbf{S}}$ is the family of orbits of the action of the group $\mathcal{H}_{\pm}(\mathbf{S})$ on $\mathbf{S}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-33 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
Since ${\mathcal S}$ is a partition of the space $\mathbf{S}$, item (1) follows from Proposition \ref{p:bsc:2}.
Item (2) follows from the fact that $\mathbf{R}\in\mathcal{H}_{-}(\mathbf{S})$, $\widetilde{\mathbf{S}}=\bbsetM\cup \mathbf{R}(M): M\in\mathbf{S}\eeset$, and item (1).
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- proposition-34: body_md -->
\label{p:bsc:4}
The following LOTS are order isomorphic to $\mathbf{S}$: $\mathbf{S} + \mathbf{S}$, $\omega \times \mathbf{S} + \mathbf{S}$, $\mathbf{S}+ \operatorname{rev} (\omega \times \mathbf{S})$.
<!-- end proposition-34 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
Let $(a,b)\in \mathfrak{J}(\mathbf{S})$. By Proposition \ref{p:bsc:1+1}, the LOTS $\ilcc[0_{\omega_1},a]$, $\ilcc[b,1_{\omega_1}]$ and $\mathbf{S}$ are order isomorphic. Hence $\mathbf{S}$ and $\mathbf{S}+\mathbf{S}$ are order isomorphic.

Take a sequence of jumps $(a_i,b_i)_{i\in\omega}\subset \mathfrak{J}(\mathbf{S})$ such that $b_i<a_{i+1}$ for $i\in\omega$. Let $b_{-1}=0_{\omega_1}$ and $b=\sup \bbsetb_i:i\in\omega\eeset$. Then $\operatorname{cf}_r(b_{i-1},\mathbf{S})=\operatorname{cf}_l(a_i,\mathbf{S})=\omega_1$ for $i\in\omega$, and $\operatorname{cf}_l(b,\mathbf{S})=\operatorname{cf}_r(1_{\omega_1},\mathbf{S})=\omega_1$. By Proposition \ref{p:bsc:1}, the LOTS $\ilcc[b_{i-1},a_i]$ for $i\in\omega$ and $\ilcc[b,1_{\omega_1}]$ are order isomorphic to $\mathbf{S}$. Hence $\ilcp[0_{\omega_1},b)$ is order isomorphic to $\omega\times \mathbf{S}$. Since $\mathbf{S}=\ilcp[0_{\omega_1},b)+\ilcc[b,1_{\omega_1}]$, $\mathbf{S}$ is order isomorphic to $\omega\times \mathbf{S} + \mathbf{S}$.

Since $\mathbf{S}$ is order isomorphic to $\operatorname{rev} \mathbf{S}$, $\mathbf{S}+ \operatorname{rev}(\omega\times \mathbf{S})$ is order isomorphic to $\operatorname{rev}(\omega\times \mathbf{S} + \mathbf{S})$. Hence $\mathbf{S}+ \operatorname{rev}(\omega\times \mathbf{S})$ is order isomorphic to $\mathbf{S}$.
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- theorem-14: body_md -->
\label{t:bsc:1}
The LOTS $\mathcal{E}_\omega(\mathbf{S}, \omega\times \mathbf{S}, \operatorname{rev}(\omega\times \mathbf{S}))$ is $\pm$-order-homogeneous.
<!-- end theorem-14 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
Let us check that the conditions of Theorem \ref{t:exos:1} hold. Since $\mathbf{S}\setminus {\mathcal B}_*(\mathbf{S})=\widetilde{\mathbf{S}}_{\omega,\omega_1}$, condition (1) of Theorem \ref{t:exos:1} follows from Proposition \ref{p:bsc:3}(2).


Let us check condition (2). Let $L=\omega\times \mathbf{S}$ and $R=\operatorname{rev}(\omega\times \mathbf{S})$, $a\in {\mathcal B}_l(X)$ and $b\in {\mathcal B}_r(X)$.

If $a=\max \mathbf{S}$, then $A=\ilpc(-\infty,a] + R + \ilpp(a,+\infty)=\mathbf{S} + \operatorname{rev}(\omega\times \mathbf{S})$. By Proposition \ref{p:bsc:4}, $A$ is order isomorphic to $\mathbf{S}$. If $a$ is a left jump point, then $A= \ilcc[0_{\omega_1},a] + \operatorname{rev}(\omega\times \mathbf{S}) + \ilcc[a',1_{\omega_1}]$, where $a'=\min \ilpp(a,+\infty)$. By Proposition \ref{p:bsc:1+1}, $A$ is order isomorphic to $\mathbf{S} + \operatorname{rev}(\omega\times \mathbf{S}) + \mathbf{S}$. By Proposition \ref{p:bsc:4}, $\mathbf{S} + \operatorname{rev}(\omega\times \mathbf{S})$ is order isomorphic to $\mathbf{S}$. Hence $A$ is order isomorphic to $\mathbf{S} + \mathbf{S}$. By Proposition \ref{p:bsc:4}, $A$ is order isomorphic to $\mathbf{S}$.

If $b=\min \mathbf{S}$, then $B=\ilpp(-\infty,b) + L + \ilcp[b,+\infty)=\omega\times \mathbf{S} + \mathbf{S}$. By Proposition \ref{p:bsc:4}, $B$ is order isomorphic to $\mathbf{S}$. If $b$ is a right jump point, then $B= \ilcc[0_{\omega_1},b'] + \omega\times \mathbf{S} + \ilcc[b,1_{\omega_1}]$, where $b'=\max \ilpp(-\infty,b)$. By Proposition \ref{p:bsc:1+1}, $A$ is order isomorphic to $\mathbf{S} + \omega\times \mathbf{S} + \mathbf{S}$. By Proposition \ref{p:bsc:4}, $\omega\times \mathbf{S}+\mathbf{S}$ is order isomorphic to $\mathbf{S}$. Hence $B$ is order isomorphic to $\mathbf{S} + \mathbf{S}$. By Proposition \ref{p:bsc:4}, $B$ is order isomorphic to $\mathbf{S}$.

By Theorem \ref{t:exos:1}, $\mathcal{E}_\omega(\mathbf{S}, \omega\times \mathbf{S}, \operatorname{rev}(\omega\times \mathbf{S}))$ is $\pm$-order-homogeneous.
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{e:1}
The group $\mathbb R^{\omega_1}$ with the order topology is a non-metrizable LOTS group that is a $P$-space.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
\label{e:2}
The Sorgenfrey line is a non-metrizable, first-countable GO paratopological group.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- example-3: body_md -->
\label{e:3}
Let $\lambda$ be a regular ordinal.
The space $X_\lambda$ is a homogeneous countably compact LOTS with $\chi(X_\lambda)=\lambda$ and $\pi\chi(X_\lambda)=\omega$.
<!-- end example-3 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
By Corollary \ref{c:blexhome:1}, the space $X_\lambda$ is homogeneous. By Proposition \ref{p:blex:1+1}, $X_\lambda$ is a countably compact LOTS with $\pi\chi(X_\lambda)=\omega$ and $\chi(X_\lambda)=\lambda$.
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- example-4: body_md -->
\label{e:4}
The space $X_{\omega_1}$ is a homogeneous countably compact LOTS with $\chi(X_{\omega_1})=\omega_1$, $\pi\chi(X_{\omega_1})=\omega$, and the transfinite line $\omega_{1}+1$ embeds in $X_{\omega_1}$.
<!-- end example-4 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
By Proposition \ref{p:blex:1+1}, the transfinite line $\omega_{1}+1$ embeds in $X_{\omega_1}$.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- example-5: body_md -->
\label{e:5}
The space $\mathbf{H}$ is a homogeneous $\sigma$-compact LOTS with $\chi(\mathbf{H})=\omega_1$ and $\pi\chi(\mathbf{H})=\omega$, and the compact space $\mathbf{S}$ embeds in $\mathbf{H}$, with $w(\mathbf{S})=c(\mathbf{S})=|\mathbf{S}|=2^{\omega_1}$ and $\chi(x,\mathbf{S})=\omega_1$ for all $x\in\mathbf{S}$.
<!-- end example-5 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
By Theorem \ref{t:bsc:1}, the space $\mathbf{H}$ is homogeneous. By Proposition \ref{p:exos:1}, $\mathbf{H}$ is $\sigma$-compact and contains the compact set $\mathbf{S}$. By Proposition \ref{p:bsc:1-1}, $w(\mathbf{S})=c(\mathbf{S})=|\mathbf{S}|=2^{\omega_1}$ and $\chi(x,\mathbf{S})=\omega_1$ for all $x\in\mathbf{S}$.
By Theorem \ref{t:main:1}, $\chi(\mathbf{H})=\omega_1$ and $\pi\chi(\mathbf{H})=\omega$.
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- question-1: body_md -->
\label{q:1-1}
Can the compact space $\mathbf{S}$ be embedded in a homogeneous countably compact LOTS? Let $K$ be a compact subset of some homogeneous countably compact LOTS. Is it true that $\chi(x,K)\leq\omega$ for some $x\in K$?
<!-- end question-1 -->
<!-- example-6: body_md -->
\label{e:6} \cite{Banakh2008}
The compact LOTS `double arrow' admits the structure of a right-topological group.
<!-- end example-6 -->
<!-- question-2: body_md -->
\label{q:1}
Does the LOTS $X_{\omega_1}$ admit the structure of a right-topological group?
<!-- end question-2 -->
<!-- question-3: body_md -->
\label{q:1+1}
Does the LOTS $\mathbf{H}$ admit the structure of a right-topological group?
<!-- end question-3 -->
<!-- question-4: body_md -->
\label{q:2}
Let $X$ be a power homogeneous GO (LOTS) space.
Is it true that every compact subset of $X$ has tightness at most $\omega_1$?
<!-- end question-4 -->
<!-- question-5: body_md -->
\label{q:3}
Let $X$ be a monotonically normal ($p$-)homogeneous space.
Is it true that every compact subset of $X$ has tightness at most $\omega_1$?
<!-- end question-5 -->
<!-- question-6: body_md -->
\label{q:4}
Let $G$ be a separable monotonically normal paratopological (semitopological, quasitopological) group. Is it true that $G$ is a stratifiable space?
<!-- end question-6 -->
<!-- question-7: body_md -->
\label{q:5}
Let $G$ be a monotonically normal topological group with countable pseudocharacter. Is it true that $G$ is a stratifiable space?
<!-- end question-7 -->
<!-- question-8: body_md -->
\label{q:6}
Let $G$ be a monotonically normal paratopological (semitopological, quasitopological) group with countable pseudocharacter. Is it true that $G$ is a stratifiable space?
<!-- end question-8 -->
<!-- question-9: body_md -->
\label{q:7}
Let $G$ be a monotonically normal topological group and let $G$ contain a convergent sequence. Is it true that $G$ is a stratifiable space?
<!-- end question-9 -->
<!-- question-10: body_md -->
\label{q:8}
Let $G$ be a monotonically normal paratopological (semitopological, quasitopological) group and let $G$ contain a convergent sequence. Is it true that $G$ is a stratifiable space?
<!-- end question-10 -->
<!-- question-11: body_md -->
\label{q:9}
Let $G$ be a monotonically normal paratopological (semitopological, quasitopological) group. Is it true that compact subsets of $G$ are metrizable (separable, first countable)?
<!-- end question-11 -->
